content.thinking:
I need to avoid writing any actual figures myself and instead use placeholder names in braces. The symptom is that cached spend totals were stale, with onset at one time but copies falling behind starting earlier, and I'm working out how to express the detection gap between the alert and the point replication stopped keeping up without inventing concrete numbers.

For the causal chain, I'm distinguishing which pieces to cite as evidence labels (T24, T21, T9, T13, T11, T15, T18) versus which are just figures I shouldn't cite directly. The root cause comes down to cache maintenance for per-shopper spend totals halting at some point, with the underlying reason for that halt remaining unidentified based on the available evidence, and I want to state that honestly rather than speculate.

Now I'm drafting contributing factors and new action items: no self-healing mechanism for stale copies (AI-3, reconcile/TTL job), late detection of the divergence (AI-4, earlier alerting on cache-vs-ledger mismatch), and empty telemetry preventing root-cause identification (AI-5, restore logging/metrics and investigate). I'm also noting that the proposed fix PR doesn't address a confirmed cause since the cause itself is unknown, so I should flag that for review rather than assume it resolves the issue.

Then for lessons learned, I'm separating what went well (fast, confirmed mitigation that held) from what went wrong (zero readable metrics/logs, unidentified cause, and a mitigation that only discards rather than prevents recurrence), while also noting the investigator's log query was anchored at a specific time window that may have missed relevant data.

For the exec summary, I want to avoid stating specific numbers — using placeholders like duration and figures instead — since impact is bounded but the actual error rate and full scope remain unknown, and the discard action only confirmed removal, not that the underlying maintenance process now works correctly.

action_items.item: Make cached spend totals correct themselves: give them an expiry, or run a periodic job that compares them with the purchase ledger and rewrites the ones that differ.

Alert as soon as cache upkeep on purchase fails or falls behind, for example on update errors or a growing count of cache entries that differ from the ledger, so the alert does not wait for a periodic comparison.
Find out why the io-shop metrics and log reads returned nothing during the incident, and restore them so an investigator can read the period around {A5}.
Find what stopped cache upkeep at {A5} by reviewing the purchase-path cache update code and the cache store's own history. Before merging the proposed fix, confirm that it addresses this trigger.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers were shown cached spend totals that disagreed with their purchases. {A1} of {A2} cached figures were wrong when the alert fired. Discarding them removed {T24.2} entries, which the store reported as the whole of what was wrong.

The cached copies were behind the purchase ledger, which was correct and unchanged. Purchases recorded since {A5} had not been applied to the copies, and nothing was putting the copies right afterwards.
The cache upkeep that should run when a purchase is recorded stopped working at {A5}, the time the copies stopped keeping up.
What stopped the upkeep is not known. No production changes were found over the windows read, no flag changes were found, and the log and metric reads came back empty. The evidence stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing repairs a stale cached total. Once upkeep stopped, each copy stayed wrong until it was discarded by hand, and every new purchase made another one stale.
Detection came late. The alert was raised {alert_raised - A5} after the copies stopped keeping up, and only because a check compared the cache to the ledger.
The investigation had no usable telemetry. Metrics and logs came back empty and the change history showed nothing, so the trigger could not be found.
The mitigation only clears the symptom. A fix has been proposed without an identified trigger, so the problem could return after the fix is merged.

input.executive_summary: Some shoppers on io-shop were shown spend totals that were out of date. The purchases themselves were recorded correctly. Only the stored copies of the totals were behind, by at least one purchase for each affected shopper. {A1} of {A2} checked totals were wrong when the alert fired, and the service had not recovered by the last metrics read, so it was broken for at least {duration}. Argus discarded the stale copies. Those pages now read from the purchase ledger, and the store confirmed it removed every entry that was wrong. The fix is not permanent. Nothing is repairing the copies, so a total will go stale again when its shopper next buys. We do not yet know why the copies stopped updating. A draft pull request has been proposed and is waiting for review.

got_lucky: The ledger never moved and the widest gap was only {A3}, with each figure missing at most {A4} purchase. The wrong totals were small and the real purchase data was not harmed.
The alert reported impact only as a lower bound, so more shoppers may have seen stale totals than the checked figures show.
went_well: Argus took the incident up straight away and discarded the stale copies. The action was confirmed, and the response was held for only {held}.
The purchase ledger was the source of truth and was untouched, so discarding the copies was safe and left nothing to put back.
A draft fix was proposed soon after mitigation.
went_wrong: The cause was not found. Metrics, logs and change history all came back empty.
The mitigation does not stop the problem coming back. Totals go stale again when their shopper next buys, and the alert said later checks would name more.
The copies had been stale since {A5} and the alert came {alert_raised - A5} later.

input.root_cause: The upkeep of the cached per-shopper spend totals (updating or invalidating the copy when a purchase is recorded) stopped working at {A5}, so the copies fell behind the purchase ledger, which stayed correct. Nothing in the change history, flag history, logs or metrics shows what stopped it, so the trigger is not identified.
